newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil BNDES denies CVRD was undervalued.
newsitem.headline: Brazil BNDES denies CVRD was undervalued.

text.p: Senior officials at Brazil's National Development Bank (BNDES) have rejected findings of a report rececently published in the press that soon-to-be-privatized mining giant CVRD was undervalued.

A minimum price of 10.361 billion reais ($9.77 billion) has been set for Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD), but the report commissioned by a Chamber of Deputies committee claimed the company was really worth 12 billion reais ($11.32 billion).

"The objective of the report was not to establish the truth, but to create a hook on which to hang the privatization process," said BNDES President Luiz Carlos Mendonca de Barros.The BNDES handles Brazilian privatizations.

A 45-percent block of CVRD voting shares is being auctioned off April 29 as the first step in the company's privatization process which has had to overcome much political opposition and several stumbling blocks.

Barros criticized the authors of the report, a group of 22 academic experts, and the lower house committee for not discussing their findings with the BNDES before publishing their "bombastic" accusations in the press.

Barros said the report made a very basic mistake in attempting to calculate the true value of CVRD by simply multiplying the company's mineral reserves by the current market price without deducting operational costs.

"They made a basic error by simply multiplying mineral reserves which lie hundreds of meters under the ground by the market price of something which is already above ground," he said. "That's what created the ... difference."
He also rejected as untrue claims that CVRD's titanium and uranium reserves were not considered in the evaluation process.
Superintendent of Privatization Tereza Cristina Aquino said titanium reserves held by CVRD did not constitute a value for the company because it was not economically viable to mine these deposits.

She said CVRD had come across traces of uranium in some of its copper or gold mines, but these represented no value because if CVRD extracted them it would have to hand them over for free to the state's nuclear monopoly, the National Commission of Nuclear Energy (CNEN).
The mining rights to any sizeable deposit of uranium found automatically go to the CNEN and therefore would also be worthless to CVRD.
((--Simona de Logu, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 507 4151))
